Neonates of the stoat (Mustela erminea) are among the smallest of the mustelids, with a reported wet weight at birth of just 2.3 grams [Wwb = 2.3 grams]. This altricial newborn emerges into the world completely helpless, its eyes sealed and its body sparsely covered in fine white hair. The initial mass is remarkably low compared to the ultimate body size the animal will achieve, reflecting a life history strategy that prioritizes a short gestation and a large litter size over the production of well-developed young. The typical gestation period for this species is 43 days [tg = 43 days] when the maternal core body temperature is maintained at 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C]. This relatively brief intrauterine development is followed by a rapid period of postnatal growth. The small birth weight imposes a high degree of dependency on the mother for thermoregulation and nutrition, and the neonate must quickly transition from the uterine environment to the demands of suckling and thermoregulation within the nest.

The period of milk dependency is a critical phase of development, during which the kit gains mass at a remarkable rate. Weaning marks a pivotal transition to nutritional independence, and field observations indicate that this milestone is achieved approximately 45 days after birth [tx = approximately 45 days after birth] under the standard thermoneutral conditions of a maternal nest at 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C]. At the point of weaning, the juvenile stoat has acquired a wet weight of roughly 26.6 grams [Wwx = roughly 26.6 grams]. This represents a more than tenfold increase from the birth weight, underscoring the efficiency of the mother’s lactation. The weaning weight is still modest compared to adult dimensions, but it is sufficient for the young stoat to begin processing solid prey, typically small rodents that the mother has begun to bring to the den. The switch from milk to meat is abrupt, and the success of this transition heavily influences the juvenile’s probability of surviving its first winter.

Sexual maturation in the stoat exhibits a remarkable degree of sexual dimorphism in timing, a phenomenon linked to the species’ polygynous mating system and the different selective pressures acting on males and females. Females attain puberty remarkably early for a mustelid of this size, becoming reproductively mature at approximately 95 days after birth [tp = approximately 95 days after birth] when their body temperature is regulated at 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C]. This allows a female born early in the spring to breed in the same summer, a strategy that maximizes lifetime reproductive output. Males, in contrast, follow a much slower developmental trajectory. They typically do not reach sexual maturity until roughly 365 days after birth [tp = roughly 365 days after birth] at the same core temperature of 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C]. This prolonged maturation in males is thought to reflect the energetic demands of achieving the larger body size required to compete successfully for territories and access to females.

The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult stoat varies considerably according to sex and geographic origin, reflecting the species’ broad Holarctic distribution and Bergmann’s rule. In many European populations, the maximum adult body mass for females is roughly 200 grams [Wwi = roughly 200 grams], a value that aligns with typical literature estimates for smaller-bodied individuals. Males in these same populations can attain a significantly greater ultimate wet weight, often reaching around 320 grams [Wwi = around 320 grams]. This nearly sixty percent difference in mass between the sexes is among the most extreme examples of sexual size dimorphism in the mustelid family. The larger body size of males is an adaptation for defending large territories that encompass the smaller, more tightly packed home ranges of several females. The dimorphism imposes distinct energetic constraints, with males requiring a higher absolute food intake and thus a larger prey base to sustain their greater mass.

The maximum reproductive output of a female stoat is constrained by both her body size and the short window of the breeding season. Under optimal conditions, a female can produce a single litter of around six to eight kits annually, and the calculation of her maximum reproductive rate, when measured as the annual number of offspring produced, yields a value of about 6.77 kits per year [Ri = about 6.77 kits per year] when her core temperature is held at 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C]. This reproductive rate is a function of producing one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year]. The lifespan of a wild stoat is relatively brief for a mammal of its size, with the maximum recorded longevity typically being around 12.5 years [am = around 12.5 years], though this extreme is rarely reached due to high mortality from predation and food scarcity at a temperature of 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C]. This maximum lifespan, measured under the same standard thermal regime of 39.6 °C [T = 39.6 °C], allows a successful female only a handful of breeding seasons in which to contribute offspring to the next generation.
